opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to focus. From day one, we've built Cohere specifically for enterprises, not for consumers. That sounds simple, but it shapes everything: what models we train, how we deploy them, and who we hire.

A lot of the big labs are chasing a consumer chatbot or a general-purpose AGI narrative, and enterprise is something of a side business for them. For us, it's the whole business. So when a bank, a telecom, or a government agency comes to us and says, "Our data can't leave our environment," we don't treat that as an edge case. We can deploy in their VPC, on-prem, even air-gapped. Data privacy and sovereignty are built into the architecture, not bolted on afterward.

Second, we're pragmatic about what actually creates value. Enterprises don't need the biggest model on every leaderboard. They need models that are efficient, that can run on a reasonable number of GPUs, that are great at retrieval, tool use, and multilingual work, and that plug into the systems they already have. That's why we invested so heavily in things like Embed and Rerank and in making our Command models strong at RAG and agentic workflows. Those are the building blocks that actually get to production.

Third, we're independent and cloud-agnostic. We're not trying to lock you into one hyperscaler. You can run Cohere on AWS, Azure, Oracle, Google, or your own hardware, which matters a lot to CIOs thinking about long-term risk.

And finally, it's the partnership itself. We work hand in hand with customers, often with our own engineers embedded alongside their teams, to get from proof of concept to something deployed across thousands of employees. The hard part of enterprise AI isn't the demo. It's the last mile, and that's where we've chosen to put our energy.

r001.rationale: The response says Cohere is independent and cloud-agnostic, with deployments on several cloud providers or customer-owned hardware.

r002.rationale: It says Cohere can deploy in a customer’s VPC, but attributes this to privacy and sovereignty requirements; it does not mention access to model weights or lack of concern about customers accessing them.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we've been pretty disciplined about who we're building for, and that's enterprises, not consumers. When you make that choice early, it shapes everything else.

A big part of it is data. The companies we work with are banks, telcos, healthcare organizations, governments. They can't send their most sensitive data off to someone else's cloud. So from the beginning we built our models to be deployable wherever the customer needs them: on their own VPC, on-prem, air-gapped if it has to be. We're not tied to a single cloud provider, and we're not trying to lock anyone into our platform. That independence matters to a lot of enterprises more than people assume.

The second piece is that we didn't just build a chatbot and hope companies would figure out what to do with it. We focused on the workloads that actually move the needle inside an organization: retrieval, search, grounding answers in a company's own documents, agents that can take actions across internal systems. Our models are trained to cite their sources and work well with retrieval-augmented generation, because in a business setting, a confident wrong answer is worse than no answer at all.

And then there's the practical side. We work closely with customers on deployment, we support a lot of languages because global enterprises are global, and we care a lot about cost and efficiency at scale. A model that's impressive in a demo but too expensive to run across ten thousand employees isn't really a product.

So I'd put it this way: we're not trying to win the race to the biggest model or the flashiest consumer app. We're trying to be the partner that enterprises can trust to put AI into production safely, privately, and in a way that actually pays off.

r001.rationale: The response says Cohere is not tied to a single cloud provider and builds models deployable wherever the customer needs them.

r002.rationale: It mentions VPC deployment, but explains it through customers’ sensitive data and deployment needs; it does not say Cohere is unconcerned about customers accessing its model weights.

I think it comes down to focus. We’re building for enterprises, and that means thinking beyond what a model can do in a demo. Can it work with your internal knowledge? Can you deploy it in a way that meets your security requirements? Can it deliver something useful at a cost that makes sense?

The model is a critical piece, but it’s not the whole solution. You need to help people connect it to their business and trust it enough to use it. That’s the kind of partner we’re trying to be: one that helps you move from experimenting with AI to making it useful in your day-to-day work.

I think it comes down to focus. We’re focused on helping enterprises put AI to work in their businesses, and that means the model is only part of the equation. It also has to work with their data, fit into their infrastructure, and meet their requirements around security and privacy.

So we think about the whole path from a promising demo to something people can reliably use every day. Can it find the right information? Can you measure whether it’s doing a good job? Can you deploy it in a way your organization is comfortable with? Our goal is to be the partner that helps companies answer those questions and turn the technology into real value.
